hookLine: crusaders sack Christian Constantinople; centuries later a pope expresses sorrow

cards: The army had taken the cross. It set out, in its own telling, to reach the Holy Land. Instead, the ships ended up under the walls of Constantinople, the great Christian city of the East, and the soldiers broke in.
Churches were stripped. Altars were looted. Christians from the West plundered Christians of the East, in the name of a holy war.
Today's story has two ends: one at those walls, and one in Athens, a very long time afterward.

teach.b: Start with what happened. Crusaders from the West were drawn into a fight over the throne of the Eastern empire. It ended with the city sacked by people baptized into the same faith in Christ as its citizens.

Pope Innocent the Third had forbidden attacks on Christians, and when he heard what was done, he wrote in anger: the Greek Church, he said, now had reason to see in the Latins only an example of ruin and the works of darkness.
He did not pretend it was a victory. Then, what it did. Before, the schism could feel like a matter of bishops and letters.
After the sack, it was memory: families, churches, a city.
In the East, the wound now had a face. Finally, the other end.
Centuries later, Pope John Paul the Second stood in Athens before the Orthodox Archbishop and named the sack of Constantinople out loud.
He said it was tragic that men who set out for the Holy Land turned against their own brothers in the faith, and that it filled Catholics with deep regret.
He asked the Lord's forgiveness for wrongs done by Catholics to Orthodox Christians.
Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims, that if your brother has something against you, leave your gift at the altar, and "go first to be reconciled to thy brother."
Sorrow, centuries later: late is not the same as never.

how: Catholic and Orthodox leaders have met, prayed together and asked forgiveness for past wrongs; Catholics who seek reconciliation often bring an old wrong to confession and then make amends where they can.

games.q: you lead a church whose people did grave harm to another church long ago. you're standing in their city. what do you do?
o: say it was all too long ago to matter.
name the wrong and say you regret it.
change the subject to their wrongs.
games.why: John Paul II named the sack out loud in Athens and spoke of Catholics' deep regret, asking the Lord's forgiveness.

practice: Let one old wrong come to mind, something you did long ago and never named; it doesn't need to be large. Don't argue your side, just name quietly what you did and who it touched.
If you pray, bring it before God and ask for the grace to say it; if the person can still be reached, you might decide when and how you'll tell them.

wordCard.voice: Constantinople. The great Christian city of the East, sacked by Western crusaders in 1204, a wound a pope later named with regret. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sorrow, centuries later. An apology can still matter, even late. I'm glad you came.
